extracted.intended_audience: regulatory scholars, policymakers, law students, and practitioners interested in behavioral economics and regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and applying Cass Sunstein's Simpler: principles and tools for designing, reviewing, and improving public regulations using behavioral economics (nudges), cost-benefit analysis, and institutional review. Emphasizes making regulation clearer, less burdensome, and evidence-informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as a guiding principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Government can be far more effective, far less confusing, far less counterproductive, and far more helpful if it opts, wherever it can, for greater simplicity (p.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to issue rules that are clearer and more accessible; simplify decision-making processes and regulatory requirements to increase freedom of choice and reduce counterproductive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nudge (preserve freedom of choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nudge defined as approaches that influence decisions while preserving freedom of choice: nudges aren't requirements, nor prohibitions or economic incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choice architecture techniques that steer decisions without coercion or bans; maintain ability for individuals to opt out or choose differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smart disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The timely release of complex information and data in standardized, machine-readable formats in ways that enable consumers to make more informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make information salient and accessible (examples: USDA Food Plate, EPA fuel economy label). Select and highlight the most decision-relevant metric (e.g., estimated US$ savings over five years for fuel economy). Use minimalist graphical representations and standardized formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic enrollment / default rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign to an agent who does not manifest his will a default choice meant to reflect what an informed, rational person would likely choose; agents remain free to opt out at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design defaults to reflect desirable informed choices. Leverage three factors for effectiveness: inertia/procrastination, perception of implicit endorsement, and establishment of reference points that interact with loss aversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–benefit analysis during design (Regulatory Moneyball)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic use of cost–benefit analysis before adoption of regulations to inform design decisions (termed 'Regulatory Moneyball').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require full access to ex ante useful information, aggregate data across agencies, and base design choices on quantified assessments rather than political expediency. Use centralized review (e.g., OIRA) to facilitate information aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–benefit analysis for monitoring (Regulatory Lookback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use cost–benefit analysis after implementation to see whether specific regulations should be revised, simplified, enhanced, or eliminated in light of their practical effect (Regulatory Lookback).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a culture of retrospective analysis: measure actual regulatory effects and revise or repeal inefficient rules based on evidence gathered post-implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized review and information-sharing (OIRA role)
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA's mission to centralize information across executive agencies and to review draft regulations; its opinions have binding force so drafts should not be issued or enforced without prior consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish institutional mechanisms to centralize regulatory information, enable cross-agency access, and provide a custodian that can enforce quality and coherence across rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations must be accessible, consistent, and in plain language
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations should be accessible, consistent, written in plain language, and easy to understand (Executive Order quote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft rules with clarity and coherence as priorities; reduce legal and practical complexity so regulated parties can understand obligations and options without undue burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base regulation on the best available science
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory decisions should be based on the best available science (Executive Order quote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use up-to-date scientific evidence to inform risk assessments and expected benefits; document scientific basis for choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow public participation and open exchange of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory system must allow for public participation and open exchange of ideas (Executive Order quote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include notice-and-comment, stakeholder engagement, and transparent disclosure of data and assumptions to enable informed participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote predictability and reduce uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation should be predictable and reduce uncertainty (Executive Order quote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rules and review processes that provide stable expectations for regulated parties and allow them to plan and comply efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the best, most innovative, and least burdensome tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and use the best, most innovative, and least burdensome tools for achieving regulatory ends (Executive Order quote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize regulatory instruments that achieve objectives with minimal compliance costs; consider information-based, default, and incentive-compatible approaches before more coercive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for benefits and costs, both quantitative and qualitative
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations must take into account benefits and costs, both quantitative and qualitative (Executive Order quote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess multiple dimensions of regulatory impacts; where quantification is difficult, provide structured qualitative analysis and transparent rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and seek to improve actual results of regulatory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory system must measure, and seek to improve, the actual results of regulatory requirements (Executive Order quote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up metrics and monitoring systems to track outcomes; use results to inform lookbacks and future rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design interventions with cognitive systems in mind (System 1 vs System 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use behavioral insights about two cognitive systems: System 1 (fast, intuitive) and System 2 (slow, deliberative) to tailor interventions—smart disclosure stimulates System 1; some strategies require policymakers to engage System 2 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose instruments that appropriately target the cognitive mode at issue: make salient cues for fast decisions, and require deliberative procedures or analyses where careful calculation is needed.
